new_statements.quote: The phonological word consists of a syllable or group of syllables with only one primary word stress. Since this stress occurs on final syllables of words in most cases and in most other cases is followed by stressless syllables which are distinguishable from pre-stress syllables of other words, symbolization of two terminals eliminates need for symbolization of primary stress. Nucleus terminal is indicated in the phonemic script by a hyphen; it occurs following primary word stress and followed by stressless syllables in the same word, which constitute a clitic. [...] Phonetically, primary stress consists of upgliding pitch and/or increased loudness. [p. 52:] Clitics do not occur with primary or secondary stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word, on the final syllable of the word in most cases; where a word ends in a clitic, the stress is on the last syllable of the word nucleus (i.e. the syllable before the stressless clitic). Primary stress is realized as a short upward pitch glide and/or extra loudness; in words of three or more syllables the initial syllable also carries some loudness and a secondary pitch glide.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Two kinds: (a) in most words of 3+ syllables the initial syllable has somewhat increased loudness and a secondary upward pitch glide, medial syllables shorter and lower (p. 50); (b) an 'independent secondary stress' of added length and loudness on a non-final syllable of certain words containing a one-syllable clitic, marked with a superscript tilde, contrastive and not predictable (pp. 50-52, n. 45; errata: freely varying in several examples).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is final 'in most cases'; in the other cases the stressed syllable is followed by stressless clitic syllables (i.e. stress is on the last syllable of the word nucleus, before the clitic), and in words with two nucleus terminals primary stress precedes the first. Secondary independent stress is lexically unpredictable ('no statement of predictability thus far proposed is valid', p. 51 n. 45; errata: 'in several of the examples given secondary stress is a freely varying phenomenon').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (a stressed 'word nucleus' plus any stressless clitics), in connected speech and citation forms; the statement is for Lower Grand Valley Dani (Hetigima/Tangma area), not measured on the mid-valley (Wamena/Mugogo) dialect; intonation-contour stress and sentence stress are separate, higher-level units (secs 3.133, 3.136).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Bromley's description of LOWER Grand Valley Dani (lowe1415 [dni]; Hetigima/Tangma area, Baliem from the Uwe to below the Muki river), a sister variety, not of midg1235 itself. Bromley (1981: 3-5) and Heider treat the Grand Valley dialects as one language, and the only first-hand description of the mid-valley dialect (van der Stap 1966, Mugogo Dani around Wamena = 'lower part of mid Grand Valley' per Bromley 1981: 5) explicitly adopts Bromley 1961 as its phonology ('there is no need for a further description', p. 2) and places Mugogo 'phonologically.. in between Bromley's Lower Aikhe Dani and his Lower Grand Valley Dani'. Bromley 1961 ch. II says nothing about stress in the mid-valley dialects (KV, BV, AV). Reviewer should decide whether to enter midg1235 on the strength of the sister-dialect statement plus van der Stap's deferral, or to leave it as 'silent for the mid-valley dialect'.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lower Grand Valley only; no phonology chapter. Ch. 1 pp. 3-5 locates the author in Hetigima/Tangma (lower valley) and van der Stap's Mugogo in 'the lower part of mid Grand Valley'. Ch. 3 notes 1 and 3 (printed p. 67): hyphen separates 'a preceding fully-stressed form from a post-cliticised form with no stress or suppressed stress'; 'Clitics are in Dani postposed units which are stressless or have suppressed stress.. (compare Bromley 1961: 49-52)'. No statement of where stress falls.
